sentences.text: The only known skull of Aquilops measures 84.2 mm in length as preserved.
Based on this skull, scientists estimate the total length of the animal was about 60 cm and its weight approximately 1.6 kg.
A fully grown individual of this species is estimated to have been one meter or less in length.
Aquilops is unique among known dinosaurs for possessing a strongly hooked rostral bone with a boss at the front edge of the snout.
This dinosaur was a plant-eater that utilized its hooked beak to nip at vegetation.
The only known specimen, a subadult skull, was discovered in 1997 in the Cloverly Formation of Carbon County, southern Montana.

In 1997, an expedition led by Richard L. Cifelli of the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, funded by the National Geographic Society, surveyed Lower Cretaceous rocks in Montana and Wyoming.
Volunteer paleontologist Scott K. Madsen found the fossil while noticing a grapefruit-sized white fragment containing teeth on a rock.
This specimen became the basis for the description of the new genus and species Aquilops americanus in 2014.
As an early ceratopsian, Aquilops is thought to have been bipedal.
The Himes Member of the Cloverly Formation, the specific layer containing Aquilops, represents a braided river system.
One study identified Aquilops as the sister taxon of Sasayamagnomus from Japan, suggesting it is one of the most basal neoceratopsians.
Aquilops is basal to a clade containing the Chinese species Auroraceratops and the Mongolian species Yamaceratops, while Liaoceratops from China is more basal than Aquilops.
A 2018 study recovered Aquilops in a polytomy with Auroraceratops and an unnamed Mongolian neoceratopsian.
A 2018 analysis dated neoceratopsian teeth from the Arundel Formation to the Aptian stage, making them older than the Albian Aquilops.
Aquilops lived in North America during the Early Cretaceous, approximately 109 to 98 million years ago.
A 2019 study by Michael D'Emic and colleagues revised the age of the formation to between 109 and 98 million years ago.
The Cloverly Formation, where Aquilops was found, is dated to either the Albian or Cenomanian stages of the Early Cretaceous.
During the Albian, much of North America was covered by vast forests with diverse plant life.
Researchers could not determine the exact age of the specimen through sectioning because limb bones, which are the most reliable indicator of growth stages, were missing.

Because only the skull was known, the body reconstruction in public artwork was based on relatives like Archaeoceratops and Psittacosaurus, relying on the assumption that early ceratopsian body plans were similar.
Prior to the description of Aquilops, the timing of dispersal and affinities of Early Cretaceous North American neoceratopsians were poorly understood.
Researchers found the evolutionary placement of Aquilops consistent with its geological age.
